The team writes in both Go and Java. New services are in Go 1.23, and the settlement engine and reconciliation batch jobs are Java 21 on Spring Boot, which is roughly 40% of the team's code, so both are in play day to day.

For the coding round, it's 60 minutes and you can pick either Go or Java.

The main one is Skeinrouter, the Go and Kafka pipeline I led at Quillhaven. It replaced a cron job that polled carrier integrations every 60 seconds, so updates arrived late and fell behind at peak. We ran 48 partitions on the main topic keyed by shipment ID to keep per-shipment ordering, an outbox table in PostgreSQL for outgoing webhooks, and backpressure by pausing partitions instead of dropping events. That took peak throughput from 9,000 to 41,000 events per second and p99 end-to-end latency from 870 ms to 140 ms.
[[GIST]] Skeinrouter: Go, Kafka, 48 partitions, outbox

I'd point to the ledger write path work I owned end to end. My part was the design and the build: idempotency keys on every write API, an outbox per service, and consumers that can be replayed safely, so money movement stays exactly-once in effect. I also owned the schema side on PostgreSQL, partitioned journal tables and serializable transactions where the invariants needed them, and I stayed with it through production and the on-call rotation afterwards.

[[GIST]] ledger write path, idempotency and outbox

The closest match is the idempotency work on Skeinrouter. I made every consumer idempotent with a dedup table in PostgreSQL keyed on event ID and carrier ID, which took duplicate webhooks from 0.6% of deliveries to under 0.01%. That's the same exactly-once-in-effect problem your ledger write path has, and I've carried the pager for a tier-1 service while owning it.

[[GIST]] idempotency, Kafka, on-call ownership

An API is a contract between two pieces of software: one side exposes a defined set of operations and data shapes, the other calls them without knowing anything about the internals. It's the boundary that lets you change what's behind it without breaking callers.

48 partitions on the main topic, keyed by shipment ID so all events for one shipment land on the same partition and keep their order.

The count came from the consumer side: one projector sustains about 1,400 events per second per partition, so the peak we planned for needed at least 30. We went to 48 for headroom, and because it divides evenly across both 12 and 16 pods.

[[GIST]] 48 partitions, keyed by shipment ID

Shipment state ended up in **PostgreSQL 15** on RDS, in the cluster we'd already moved to during Marrowgate, with the shipment_state table hash-partitioned into 32 partitions. We considered a managed key-value store and set it aside, because the outbox needs one transaction covering the state change and the outgoing message, and the shipments in transit fit in memory on one PostgreSQL primary. The design doc's earlier DynamoDB idea didn't survive that reasoning. The rule we hold to is that shipment-projector is the only writer of shipment state, and the monolith reads it through a gRPC read API.

[[GIST]] PostgreSQL, not DynamoDB, for the outbox transaction

Skeinrouter is five Go services on Amazon MSK, Kafka 3.6, six brokers across three AZs. The main topic, tracking.raw, has 48 partitions keyed by shipment ID, which is what gives us per-shipment ordering without any coordination between consumers. I wrote the partitioning and ordering scheme, the shared consumer framework, and the deduplication layer, and I reviewed every change to the delivery path.

[[GIST]] 48 partitions keyed by shipment ID

The reason was per-shipment ordering and replay. Keying on shipment ID gives us ordering without coordinating consumers, and events stay on the topic so we can reprocess history. We turned down SQS FIFO, which has a throughput ceiling per message group and no replay, and RabbitMQ, which has no replay and needs a single consumer per queue for strict ordering. We also rejected partitioning by carrier, since the largest carrier is only 9% of traffic and that would have made one partition permanently hot.

[[GIST]] ordering, replay; rejected SQS FIFO, RabbitMQ

Offsets are committed only after the database transaction commits, so a pod dying mid-batch just means its partitions move to another member of the group, which re-reads from the last committed offset. At most one batch, up to 500 records, gets processed again, and the deduplication table turns those repeats into no-ops. Nothing is lost and nothing is applied twice.

[[GIST]] re-read from last committed offset, deduped

The worst one was a consumer-lag incident on our tracking pipeline at Quillhaven, in November 2024. We were mid-rollout, 720 carriers already live, and a routine rolling restart of the projector pods triggered a rebalance storm: the group was still on eager rebalancing, so every pod restart stopped the whole group, and once the database was absorbing the backlog a batch could exceed the 30-second max.poll.interval, members got evicted for being slow, and each eviction caused another rebalance.

I took incident command at 14:20, we raised it to Sev-1 at 15:30 with lag peaking at 96 million events and the worst shipments 47 minutes behind. We paused the deploy, scaled the group down to 8 pods, and raised max.poll.interval to 5 minutes, which stabilised it. Backlog drained by 17:45, so 3 hours 40 minutes total. No events lost, nothing rolled back, because the deduplication table kept the repeats out.

The follow-up mattered more: we moved every consumer group to cooperative rebalancing with static membership, made rolling restarts go one pod at a time behind a lag gate, and put a burn-rate alert on consumer lag.

[[GIST]] rebalance storm, 3h40m, fixed with cooperative rebalancing

Straight answer: the outbox part is a close match, the idempotency-keys-on-write-APIs part is not.

On the outbox, Skeinrouter has one. The shipment-projector writes the state change and the outbox row in the same PostgreSQL transaction, and outbox-relay reads it with SKIP LOCKED and publishes. That's the pattern the JD describes, and I owned the design.

On idempotency, what I built is consumer-side dedup, not producer-side idempotency keys. The processed_events table is keyed on event ID and carrier ID, and it's what makes replays safe. That's the "consumers that can be replayed safely" half. What I haven't done is put a client-supplied idempotency key on every write endpoint, which is the other half and the one that matters more in a payments ledger.

So I'd say I'm strong on the outbox and replay-safety, and I'd be learning the write-API idempotency layer on the job.

[[GIST]] outbox yes, write-API idempotency keys no

No, it's not safe. TryConsume reads the counter under a read lock, releases it, then writes under a write lock, so two goroutines for the same tenant can both read the same value and both pass the check. It's a classic check-then-act race, and it overshoots the limit under concurrent load. The fix is to do the read, compare and increment under one write lock, or use an atomic per-tenant counter.

I've hit this shape of bug for real. On Skeinrouter I made every consumer idempotent with a deduplication table in PostgreSQL keyed on event ID and carrier ID, which cut duplicate status webhooks from 0.6% of deliveries to under 0.01%.

[[GIST]] check-then-act race, needs one lock

The bug is that `upper` is treated as a per-tier width instead of a cumulative boundary. `min(remaining, upper)` should be `min(remaining, upper - previous_upper)`, so each tier only charges the units between its lower and upper bound. For 12000 units it should return **340000 mills**: 1000 at 50, 9000 at 30, 2000 at 10.

## Approach
Two pointers, one from each end, skipping anything that isn't a letter or digit and comparing lowercased characters. That gives linear time and constant extra space, which is what the sheet asks for. I'll use `str.isalnum()` to decide what to skip.

## Code
```python
def is_palindrome(s):
    left, right = 0, len(s) - 1
    while left < right:
        while left < right and not s[left].isalnum():
            left += 1
        while left < right and not s[right].isalnum():
            right -= 1
        if s[left].lower() != s[right].lower():
            return False
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return True
```

## Complexity
Time is O(n), each character is visited at most once by the two pointers. Space is O(1), just the two indices.

[[GIST]] two pointers, skip non-alnum, O(1) space

Time is O(n), since each pointer moves inward and every character is looked at at most once. Space is O(1), just the two indices. And yes, this already does it without a second string. I never build a filtered copy, I skip non-alphanumerics in place and compare lowercased characters directly, so the only extra memory is the two pointers.

[[GIST]] O(n) time, O(1) space, no copy

I'm primary on-call for the dispatch domain one week in five, and I've been incident commander on 9 Sev-1 and Sev-2 incidents since April 2024. The load's come down a lot: we took Sev-1s in the domain from 14 in 2023 to 5 in 2025, and median time to restore from 52 minutes to 19.

[[GIST]] one week in five, 9 incidents led

I start from the user journey, not the infrastructure. For a new service I'd ask what the caller actually experiences, pick the one or two signals that track that, and set the target from what we can defend today rather than an aspirational number. Then I'd validate it against real traffic, and treat it as a starting point we tighten as we learn. On the dispatch pipeline I replaced threshold alerts with burn-rate alerts once we had a target worth defending.

The deciding factor was how often each piece of data changes. The clinic page and service list are server-rendered so the largest element is already in the HTML, and clinic profiles use incremental static regeneration with a 300-second revalidation because they change a few times a week. Slots are the opposite, so they're fetched in the browser and never cached longer than 30 seconds, since a stale slot is a double booking waiting to happen. We did prototype just splitting the bundle, but mobile LCP only got to 3.1 seconds, so it wasn't enough.

[[GIST]] render by data volatility, not client-only

The Fernlatch booking flow, back in March 2023. I was tech lead on the rebuild, and release 0.19 formatted slot times during server rendering. The server formatted them in its own time zone and the browser formatted them again in the clinic's, so where the two differed the markup didn't match, React threw away the server-rendered tree and re-rendered in the browser, and for clinics outside the server's zone the first paint showed slots an hour off. Interaction delay at p75 went from 130 ms to 410 ms while it was live, and 312 bookings were made at the wrong hour in the 26 hours before we caught it. A support ticket from a clinic in the Azores and a real-user-monitoring alert landed within minutes of each other, and we rolled back 25 minutes after detection. Support contacted every affected clinic and owner within two days. The fix sends slots as ISO strings with the clinic's time zone and formats them only in the browser after mount, and we added a Playwright run in three time zones plus a rule that any hydration error fails the build. What I'd change is putting that multi-time-zone run in place before the first server-rendered release, not after.

[[GIST]] time-zone hydration bug, rollback, three-zone tests

On Fernlatch, the booking flow, I was tech lead of three frontend engineers. We rebuilt it in React and TypeScript with server rendering on Next.js, route-level code splitting, and image sizing at build time. Mobile p75 LCP went from 4.3 seconds to 1.7, interaction delay from 380 ms to 120 ms, and first-load JavaScript from 1.9 MB to 610 kB. We enforced a 650 kB budget on the booking route in Lighthouse CI, blocking any pull request that added more than 25 kB. On your 350 kB target, that's a real gap, and I'd want to know what's in your baseline before I say how close we are.

[[GIST]] 610 kB shipped, 350 kB target

SMS is 5% of 180 million a day, so 9 million SMS a day. Average is about 104 per second, and at 6x peak that's roughly 625 per second, which is over the vendor's 500 per second cap. So yes, I need a buffer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    api["Send API"] -->|"enqueue"| queue["Notification Queue"]
    queue --> router["Channel Router"]
    router -->|"70% push"| push["Push Provider"]
    router -->|"25% email"| email["Email Provider"]
    router -->|"5% SMS"| sms["SMS Queue"]
    sms -->|"token bucket, 500/s"| vendor["SMS Vendor"]
    sms -->|"attempts exhausted"| dlq["Dead-Letter Queue"]
```

The router splits by channel, and SMS goes into its own queue drained by a worker with a token bucket at 500 per second. That absorbs the burst: at 625 per second incoming against 500 out, the queue grows by about 125 a second, so a burst of a few minutes is a few tens of thousands of messages of backlog, which drains shortly after the peak. Transactional SMS still needs to hit the 2 second p99, so I'd give it a priority lane ahead of promotional traffic. The tradeoff is added latency and a queue to operate, but the alternative is dropping or throttling sends at exactly the moment campaigns fire.

The problem is the N+1: one query for the members, then two more per member inside the loop, so a 250-person team is about **501 round trips**.

The fix is to batch it: one query for members, then one grouped query for task counts and one for last logins, keyed by member id. That's **3 round trips**, and it stays flat as the team grows.

[[GIST]] N+1 loop, 501 trips to 3

I don't have a specific pipeline of my own to walk you through, so let me be straight about that rather than invent one. What I can do is design one with you right now, and I'll be explicit about which choices are mine versus what I'd validate against real numbers.

For an event pipeline, the first thing I'd pin down is the contract: what's the event, what's the key, and what ordering guarantee actually matters downstream. Topics usually fall out of that. I'd separate by domain and by consumer need, so a high-volume firehose topic doesn't force every consumer to filter through it. Something like raw ingestion per source, then a cleaned or enriched topic, then per-consumer topics where the access patterns genuinely differ.

Partitioning follows the key. If I need per-entity ordering, I partition on that entity id so all events for one entity land on one partition and stay ordered. If ordering doesn't matter, I'd spread on a high-cardinality key to avoid hot partitions. Partition count is a throughput and parallelism decision, so I'd size it from measured bytes per second per partition and the consumer's processing rate, not a guess.

Throughput I'd only quote after load testing, because it depends on message size, replication factor, batch settings, and how fast consumers commit. What I'd watch is consumer lag and partition skew, since a single hot partition caps you no matter how many you have.

If you want, give me the shape of your system and I'll get concrete on topic names and partition keys.
